docs.title: Keras Probability
docs.text:
Uncertainty awareness for deep learning in Keras 3.

keras_proba gives Keras models calibrated, distance-aware uncertainty estimates. Every layer, loss and metric runs on the TensorFlow, JAX and PyTorch backends, plugs into model.compile / model.fit, and saves with model.save.

The distance-aware and Bayesian layers are ports of TensorFlow Model Garden and TensorFlow Probability, tested for numerical parity with them.

docs.title: What's inside
docs.text: Need Use A classifier that knows when inputs are far from the training data SNGP: SpectralNormalization + RandomFeatureGaussianProcess, or the all-in-one GaussianProcessClassificationHead Uncertainty over the weights Bayesian layers: DenseFlipout, DenseReparameterization, Conv{1,2,3}DFlipout, ... Regression with a predicted noise level GaussianHead with GaussianNLL Multi-modal or skewed regression targets MixtureGaussianHead with MixtureGaussianNLL Measuring calibration ExpectedCalibrationError, BrierScore Fixing an overconfident trained classifier TemperatureScaling Intervals or sets with a coverage guarantee SplitConformalRegressor, SplitConformalClassifier

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install keras-proba

Keras 3 needs one backend; install it with an extra, e.g. pip install "keras-proba[jax]" ([torch], [jax] or [tensorflow]).

docs.title: A first example
docs.text:
A classifier whose predictions become uncertain away from the training data:

import numpy as np
import keras
import keras_proba

x = np.random.normal(size=(512, 2)).astype("float32")
y = (x[:, 0] * x[:, 1] > 0).astype("int32")

inputs = keras.Input((2,))
hidden = keras.layers.Dense(64, trainable=False)(inputs)  # A frozen random projection.
hidden = keras_proba.layers.SpectralNormalization(keras.layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"))(hidden)
logits = keras_proba.layers.GaussianProcessClassificationHead(
    inner_dim=0,
    num_classes=2,
    temperature=np.pi / 8,
    normalize_input=False,
    scale_random_features=True,
    custom_random_features_initializer=keras.initializers.RandomNormal(stddev=1.0),
)(hidden)
model = keras.Model(inputs, logits)

model.compile(
    optimizer="adam",
    loss=keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True),
    metrics=["accuracy", keras_proba.metrics.ExpectedCalibrationError(from_logits=True)],
)
model.fit(x, y, epochs=10, verbose=0, callbacks=[keras_proba.callbacks.ResetCovarianceCallback()])

probs = keras.ops.softmax(model.predict(np.array([[0.5, 0.5], [8.0, -8.0]], "float32"), verbose=0))
# Confident near the data, close to uniform far from it.

Continue with Getting Started, jump to a guide, or run an example notebook on Google Colab.

docs.title: Verified against the references
docs.text:
Each component is tested on all three backends for:

  • Parity with the original implementation (Model Garden, TensorFlow Probability, PyTorch, SciPy), feeding both the same weights and random draws.
  • Training: the method does its job on real fits, e.g. out-of-distribution uncertainty, improved calibration, or the theoretical conformal coverage.
  • Serialization: model.save / keras.models.load_model round trips.

See Testing for details, including the bugs in the references that these tests surfaced.

docs.title: Choosing your backend
docs.text:
keras_proba runs on every Keras 3 backend. Set KERAS_BACKEND before importing Keras:

PyTorchJAXTensorFlow 
import os
os.environ["KERAS_BACKEND"] = "torch"
import keras

import os
os.environ["KERAS_BACKEND"] = "jax"
import keras

import os
os.environ["KERAS_BACKEND"] = "tensorflow"
import keras

JAX and spectral normalization

In its default mode="projection", SpectralNormalization behaves like the reference only on TensorFlow and PyTorch. Use mode="reparameterization" for identical behavior on every backend; see the SNGP guide.

docs.title: From a model to calibrated uncertainty
docs.text:
A typical workflow on a classifier:

import numpy as np
import keras
from keras_proba import metrics, postprocessing

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.normal(size=(3000, 10)).astype("float32")
y = (x[:, :3] @ rng.normal(size=(3, 4)) + rng.normal(size=(3000, 4))).argmax(-1)
(x_train, y_train), (x_cal, y_cal), (x_test, y_test) = [(x[s], y[s]) for s in (slice(0, 1500), slice(1500, 2200), slice(2200, None))]

# 1. Train, tracking calibration alongside accuracy.
model = keras.Sequential([keras.Input((10,)), keras.layers.Dense(128, activation="relu"), keras.layers.Dense(4)])
model.compile(
    optimizer="adam",
    loss=keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True),
    metrics=["accuracy", metrics.ExpectedCalibrationError(from_logits=True)],
)
model.fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=30, verbose=0)

# 2. Calibrate the confidence on held-out data.
scaling = postprocessing.TemperatureScaling()
scaling.fit(model.predict(x_cal, verbose=0), y_cal)
calibrated = keras.Sequential([model, scaling])

# 3. Turn predictions into sets that contain the label 90% of the time.
probs_cal = keras.ops.softmax(calibrated.predict(x_cal, verbose=0))
conformal = postprocessing.SplitConformalClassifier(alpha=0.1, score="aps").fit(y_cal, probs_cal)
sets = conformal.predict_set(keras.ops.softmax(calibrated.predict(x_test, verbose=0)))
print(float(postprocessing.set_coverage(y_test, sets)), float(postprocessing.average_set_size(sets)))

Calibration and conformal prediction work on any trained classifier. To also make the model itself uncertainty-aware, use an SNGP head or Bayesian layers.

docs.title: Saving and loading
docs.text:
Every layer, loss and metric is registered with Keras, so models save and load as usual:

calibrated.save("calibrated.keras")
restored = keras.models.load_model("calibrated.keras")

Fitted conformal predictors are plain Python objects; save them with their JSON-compatible get_config() and restore them with from_config.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
The test suite runs once per backend:

pip install -e ".[dev]"
KERAS_BACKEND=jax pytest          # Or torch, tensorflow.

docs.title: Test categories
docs.text: Folder What it checks tests/tests_parity Numerical parity with the original implementation, given the same weights and random draws. tests/tests_smoke Shapes, analytic values, invariants, error handling and the public API. tests/tests_training That each method does its job when trained: out-of-distribution uncertainty, improved calibration, conformal coverage of exactly \(k / (n + 1)\), ... tests/tests_serialization get_config / from_config and model.save / keras.models.load_model round trips.

The Model Garden and TensorFlow Probability parity tests load the reference sources from a local reference/ folder (not distributed with the package) and are skipped when it is absent, as in CI. RandomFourierFeatures parity only needs tf_keras.

docs.title: Differences from the references
docs.text:
Some deviations are deliberate, each covered by a test:

  • Brier decomposition: TFP's brier_decomposition indexes the average label distribution by the predicted class in its resolution term. keras_proba uses the textbook formula, for which uncertainty − resolution + reliability reproduces the Brier score exactly when all predictions with the same argmax are identical; TFP's can be off by up to 0.39.
  • Quantile-bucket ECE: bucket edges are data points, and TFP compares log-probabilities with edges that went through exp and log, so a point on an edge can fall in either bucket depending on float rounding. keras_proba compares in probability space, where an edge equals its data point exactly.
  • Local reparameterization: an all-zero input gives a NaN scale gradient in TFP; a tiny constant under the square root keeps it finite.
  • Spectral normalization on JAX: see the SNGP guide.
  • Robustness: the GP and SNGP head unpack every output combination (return_gp_cov=False, return_random_features=True) and accept rank-2 features, where the reference crashes.

docs.title: ResetCovarianceCallback
docs.text:
Bases: keras.src.callbacks.callback.Callback

Resets the precision matrix of every GP covariance layer at the start of each epoch.

RandomFeatureGaussianProcess accumulates its posterior precision matrix over training minibatches. Since the feature extractor changes during training, the estimate should be recomputed in each epoch, so that the final covariance only reflects the last epoch's features [1].

Example:

model.fit(x, y, epochs=10, callbacks=[ResetCovarianceCallback()])

[1]: Jeremiah Liu et al. Simple and Principled Uncertainty Estimation with Deterministic Deep Learning via Distance Awareness. In Neural Information Processing Systems, 2020. https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.10108

docs.title: RandomFourierFeatures
docs.text:
RandomFourierFeatures(output_dim, kernel_initializer='gaussian', scale=None, trainable=False, name=None, **kwargs)

Bases: keras.src.layers.layer.Layer

Projects inputs into a random feature space approximating an RBF kernel.

Typically used to "kernelize" a linear model: a linear layer trained on top of these features is (up to approximation) a kernel machine, e.g. kernel logistic regression or the random feature Gaussian process used in SNGP.

Example:

model = keras.Sequential([
    keras.Input(shape=(784,)),
    RandomFourierFeatures(output_dim=4096, scale=10.0),
    keras.layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax"),
])

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default output_dim

Positive integer, the number of random features D.

required kernel_initializer

"gaussian", "laplacian" (case insensitive), or a Keras initializer for the random feature kernel W. The kernel is never trainable.

'gaussian' scale

Positive float, the kernel length scale. If None, defaults to sqrt(input_dim / 2) for "gaussian" and 1.0 otherwise. If trainable=True, it is learned and this is its initial value.

None trainable

Whether scale is trainable. Defaults to False.

False name

String, name of the layer.

None Input shape

(..., input_dim) with a defined last dimension. Unlike the reference, inputs of rank greater than 2 are supported.

Output shape

(..., output_dim).

RandomFeatureGaussianProcess(units, num_inducing=1024, gp_kernel_type='gaussian', gp_kernel_scale=1.0, gp_output_bias=0.0, normalize_input=False, gp_kernel_scale_trainable=False, gp_output_bias_trainable=False, gp_cov_momentum=0.999, gp_cov_ridge_penalty=1.0, scale_random_features=True, use_custom_random_features=True, custom_random_features_initializer=None, custom_random_features_activation=None, l2_regularization=1e-06, gp_cov_likelihood='gaussian', return_gp_cov=True, return_random_features=False, dtype=None, name=None, trainable=True, **gp_output_kwargs)

Bases: keras.src.layers.layer.Layer

Gaussian process layer with random feature approximation [1].

During training, the layer updates the maximum a posteriori (MAP) logits and the posterior precision matrix using minibatch statistics. During inference, it also returns the predictive covariance, which can be used to compute posterior mean probabilities via mean_field_logits.

Different random features can be used by setting use_custom_random_features=True and changing the initializer and activation of the custom random features. For example:

MLP kernel: initializer="random_normal", activation="relu"
RBF kernel: initializer="random_normal", activation=keras.ops.cos

A linear kernel can be used with gp_kernel_type="linear" and use_custom_random_features=True.

Example:

inputs = keras.Input(shape=(128,))
logits, covmat = RandomFeatureGaussianProcess(units=10)(inputs)
probs = keras.ops.softmax(mean_field_logits(logits, covmat, math.pi / 8))

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default units

Number of output units.

required num_inducing

Number of random Fourier features.

1024 gp_kernel_type

Kernel type. "gaussian" (RBF) by default, or "linear" when use_custom_random_features=True.

'gaussian' gp_kernel_scale

Length scale of the kernel, i.e. for the RBF kernel exp(-|x1 - x2|**2 / gp_kernel_scale).

1.0 gp_output_bias

Initial value of the output bias.

0.0 normalize_input

Whether to apply layer normalization to the input.

Whether the length scale is trainable. Only used when use_custom_random_features=False.

False gp_output_bias_trainable

Whether the output bias is trainable.

Discount factor of the moving average of the precision matrix. If not positive, minibatch precision matrices are summed instead, which gives the exact precision after one pass over the data.

Computes the Gaussian process covariance using the Laplace method.

At training time, this layer updates the Gaussian process posterior using model features in minibatches.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default momentum

Ridge penalty of the initial precision matrix. It stabilizes the inverse inv(t(X) X + s I), but should not be so large that it dominates t(X) X.

inputs: GP random features of shape (batch_size, num_features). logits: Pre-activation output of shape (batch_size, 1). Required for non-Gaussian likelihoods. training: Whether to update the precision matrix.

Returns:

Type Description

Identity of shape (batch_size, batch_size) during training, and the

predictive covariance of the same shape during inference.

docs.title: compute_predictive_covariance
docs.text:
compute_predictive_covariance(gp_feature)

Computes the posterior predictive covariance.

Given training random features Phi_tr of shape (num_train, num_hidden) and test random features Phi_ts of shape (batch_size, num_hidden), the predictive covariance (assuming a Gaussian likelihood) is:

s * Phi_ts @ inv(t(Phi_tr) * Phi_tr + s * I) @ t(Phi_ts),

where s is the ridge penalty used to stabilize the inverse.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default gp_feature

Random features of the test data, shape (batch_size, num_hidden).

required

Returns:

Type Description

Predictive covariance matrix of shape (batch_size, batch_size).

Bases: keras_proba.layers.classification_head.ClassificationHead

Gaussian process-based pooling head for classification (SNGP) [1].

It applies spectral normalization to the hidden pooler layer, and replaces the dense output layer with a random feature Gaussian process. During training it returns the raw logits; at inference it returns logits adjusted with mean_field_logits, and optionally the covariance matrix.

Remember to reset the GP covariance at the start of each epoch, e.g. with keras_proba.callbacks.ResetCovarianceCallback.

Example:

inputs = keras.Input((128,))
hidden = keras.layers.Dense(128, activation="relu")(inputs)
head = GaussianProcessClassificationHead(inner_dim=128, num_classes=10, temperature=math.pi / 8)
model = keras.Model(inputs, head(hidden))

Name Type Description Default inner_dim

required num_classes

required cls_token_idx

0 activation

Activation of the inner projection layer.

'tanh' dropout_rate

Dropout probability before the output projection.

0.0 initializer

Initializer for the dense layer kernels.

'glorot_uniform' use_spec_norm

Whether to apply spectral normalization to the pooler layer.

True use_gp_layer

Whether to use a Gaussian process as the output layer.

True temperature

Mean-field factor used at inference. If None, no mean-field adjustment is applied.

None **kwargs

docs.title: expected_calibration_error_quantiles
docs.text:
expected_calibration_error_quantiles(hit, pred_log_prob, num_buckets=20, axis=0, log_space_buckets=False)

Expected calibration error over equal-count buckets of predicted probability.

A model is calibrated if buckets of predicted probabilities have the same within-bucket average accuracy. The ECE is the average absolute difference between predicted probability and bucket accuracy:

bucket_weight = bucket_count / sum(bucket_count)
bucket_error = abs(bucket_accuracy - bucket_confidence)
ece = sum(bucket_weight * bucket_error)

where buckets are num_buckets-quantiles of exp(pred_log_prob).

Example:

hit = [False, False, True, False, True, True]
log_pred = np.log([0.1, 0.05, 0.5, 0.2, 0.99, 0.99])
ece, acc, conf, cnt, edges, bucket = expected_calibration_error_quantiles(hit, log_pred, num_buckets=3)
# ece  ==> 0.145
# acc  ==> [0., 0., 1.]
# conf ==> [0.075, 0.2, 0.826665]
# cnt  ==> [2., 1., 3.]

For a probability vector p and a realized outcome k, the Brier score is sum_i p[i]^2 - 2 p[k]. Smaller values are better. It is a strictly proper scoring rule, and can be negative. This form differs from sum_i (p[i] - onehot(k)[i])^2 by a constant of 1.

docs.title: brier_decomposition
docs.text:
brier_decomposition(labels, logits)

Decomposes the Brier score into uncertainty, resolution, and reliability.

Any proper scoring rule admits a unique decomposition as Score = Uncertainty - Resolution + Reliability, where:

  • Uncertainty is a generalized entropy of the average predictive distribution; it can be positive or negative.
  • Resolution is a generalized variance of individual predictive distributions; it is always non-negative, and larger is better.
  • Reliability measures calibration of predictions against the true frequency of events; it is always non-negative, and lower is better.

The space of predictive distributions is discretized by their argmax. The estimation error of each component is O(k/n) for n instances and k labels.

Note: TFP's implementation computes the resolution as sum_k w_k sum_j (pbar[k] - dist_mean[k, j])^2, indexing the average label distribution by the predicted class. Here it is sum_k w_k sum_j (pbar[j] - dist_mean[k, j])^2, for which the decomposition reproduces the Brier score exactly when all predictions with the same argmax are identical. Uncertainty and reliability match TFP.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default labels

Integer tensor of shape (..., n) with class labels.

required logits

Tensor of shape (..., n, num_classes).

required

Returns:

Type Description

Tuple of uncertainty, resolution and reliability, each of shape

(...).

docs.text:
SplitConformalRegressor(alpha=0.1)

Split conformal prediction intervals for regression.

Without scale, the score is the absolute residual |y - y_pred| and intervals have a constant width 2 q_hat. With a per-example scale (e.g. the standard deviation of a GaussianHead, MixtureGaussianHead or Monte Carlo samples), the score is |y - y_pred| / scale and intervals y_pred +- q_hat * scale adapt to each input [2]. Each output dimension gets its own threshold, so coverage holds for each dimension separately.

Example:

mean, scale = split_gaussian_params(model.predict(x_cal))
conformal = SplitConformalRegressor(alpha=0.1).fit(y_cal, mean, scale=scale)
mean, scale = split_gaussian_params(model.predict(x_test))
lower, upper = conformal.predict_interval(mean, scale=scale)

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default alpha

Miscoverage level in (0, 1); intervals cover with probability at least 1 - alpha.

    ```python
    mean, scale = split_gaussian_params(model.predict(x_test))
    lower, upper = conformal.predict_interval(mean, scale=scale)
    ```

docs.text:
SplitConformalClassifier(alpha=0.1, score='lac', from_logits=False, randomized=True, seed=None)

Split conformal prediction sets for classification.

Scores:

  • "lac" (least ambiguous set-valued classifier): 1 - p_label. Sets are {k : p_k >= 1 - q_hat}, with exact coverage and the smallest average size [2]; they can be empty for ambiguous inputs.
  • "aps" (adaptive prediction sets) [3]: the probability mass of the classes ranked before the label, plus u * p_label. Sets grow with the model's uncertainty about each input. With randomized=True (default), u ~ Uniform(0, 1) and sets {k : mass before k + u * p_k <= q_hat} have exact coverage. With randomized=False, u = 1 and the sets {k : mass before k < q_hat} are never empty but conservative: on hard tasks they can cover far more than 1 - alpha.

Example:

conformal = SplitConformalClassifier(alpha=0.1, score="aps").fit(y_cal, model.predict(x_cal))
sets = conformal.predict_set(model.predict(x_test))  # Boolean, (n, num_classes).

percentile(x, q, axis=None, interpolation=None, keepdims=False)

Computes the q-th percentile(s) of x.

Given a vector x, the q-th percentile is the value q / 100 of the way from the minimum to the maximum in a sorted copy of x. The two nearest neighbors and interpolation determine the result when the normalized rank does not match a sample exactly. Compare to numpy.percentile.

Example:

x = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]

percentile(x, q=30.0, interpolation="linear")  # 1.9
percentile(x, q=[30.0, 70.0], interpolation="lower")  # [1.0, 3.0]
percentile([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]], q=100.0, axis=[0])  # [3.0, 4.0]

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default x

Numeric tensor with at least one dimension.

required q

Scalar or 1-D percentile(s) in [0, 100], as concrete values.

required axis

None interpolation

One of "nearest" (default), "linear", "lower", "higher" or "midpoint", used when a percentile lies between samples i < j: i + (j - i) * fraction, i, j, the nearest of the two, or (i + j) / 2. "linear" and "midpoint" require a floating point x.

None keepdims

Whether to keep the reduced axes with size 1.

False

docs.title: A Bayesian CNN: asking a network several times
docs.text:
Backend: TensorFlow, JAX or PyTorch Dataset: Fashion-MNIST, MNIST Techniques: Conv2DFlipout, DenseFlipout

View in Colab GitHub source

Average a Bayesian CNN's repeated predictions, and use their disagreement to flag unfamiliar inputs.

A Bayesian network learns a distribution over its weights instead of a single value. Each prediction samples new weights, like asking a slightly different expert. When the experts agree, the network is sure; when they disagree, it is not. Two benefits follow:

  • Averaging several predictions is usually more accurate than any single one.
  • The disagreement between them measures what the network does not know, and flags inputs unlike the training data.

Here, a Bayesian CNN learns Fashion-MNIST and is then shown MNIST digits.

# Install keras-proba, then choose a backend: "jax", "tensorflow" or "torch".
!pip install -q keras-proba
import os

os.environ["KERAS_BACKEND"] = "jax"

docs.title: Load the data
docs.text:
Fashion-MNIST clothing images for training and testing, and MNIST digits as unfamiliar inputs.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

import keras
import keras_proba

keras.utils.set_random_seed(0)
(x_train, y_train), (x_test, y_test) = keras.datasets.fashion_mnist.load_data()
(_, _), (x_digits, _) = keras.datasets.mnist.load_data()
x_train, x_test, x_digits = (images[..., None].astype("float32") / 255 for images in (x_train, x_test, x_digits))

docs.title: A Bayesian CNN
docs.text:
Conv2DFlipout and DenseFlipout are the Bayesian versions of Conv2D and Dense. Training fits the data while keeping each weight distribution close to a prior; kl_weight (the standard choice is 1 / number of training examples) sets how much the prior counts.

kl_weight = 1.0 / len(x_train)
model = keras.Sequential(
    [
        keras.Input((28, 28, 1)),
        keras_proba.layers.Conv2DFlipout(16, 3, padding="same", activation="relu", kl_weight=kl_weight),
        keras.layers.MaxPooling2D(),
        keras_proba.layers.Conv2DFlipout(32, 3, padding="same", activation="relu", kl_weight=kl_weight),
        keras.layers.MaxPooling2D(),
        keras.layers.Flatten(),
        keras_proba.layers.DenseFlipout(128, activation="relu", kl_weight=kl_weight),
        keras_proba.layers.DenseFlipout(10, kl_weight=kl_weight),
    ]
)
model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss=keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True), metrics=["accuracy"])
model.fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=5, batch_size=128, verbose=0)

docs.title: Ask the network 20 times
docs.text:
Every predict call samples new weights. We keep all 20 predicted class distributions.

def predict_samples(x, num_samples=20):
    logits = [model.predict(x, batch_size=512, verbose=0) for _ in range(num_samples)]
    return np.stack([keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(keras.ops.softmax(l)) for l in logits])  # (samples, images, classes)


samples_test, samples_digits = predict_samples(x_test), predict_samples(x_digits)
single = (samples_test[0].argmax(-1) == y_test).mean()
averaged = (samples_test.mean(0).argmax(-1) == y_test).mean()
print(f"Accuracy: one prediction {single:.1%}, average of 20 predictions {averaged:.1%}")

Accuracy: one prediction 87.5%, average of 20 predictions 88.9%

docs.title: Measure the disagreement
docs.text:
The mutual information between the predictions and the weights measures how much the 20 predictions disagree: the entropy of their average minus their average entropy. It is near zero when all samples predict the same thing, and large when they contradict each other.

def entropy(p):
    return -np.sum(p * np.log(p + 1e-12), axis=-1)


def mutual_information(samples):
    return entropy(samples.mean(0)) - entropy(samples).mean(0)


plt.figure(figsize=(7, 3))
plt.hist(mutual_information(samples_test), bins=50, range=(0, 1), alpha=0.6, density=True, label="clothing (seen)")
plt.hist(mutual_information(samples_digits), bins=50, range=(0, 1), alpha=0.6, density=True, label="digits (never seen)")
plt.xlabel("disagreement between the 20 predictions (mutual information)")
plt.legend()
plt.show()


def auroc(familiar, unfamiliar):
    ranks = np.concatenate([familiar, unfamiliar]).argsort().argsort() + 1
    n, m = len(familiar), len(unfamiliar)
    return (ranks[n:].sum() - m * (m + 1) / 2) / (n * m)


print(f"Disagreement separates digits from clothing with AUROC {auroc(mutual_information(samples_test), mutual_information(samples_digits)):.3f} (0.5 = chance)")


Disagreement separates digits from clothing with AUROC 0.874 (0.5 = chance)

docs.title: What we learned
docs.text:
• Bayesian layers are drop-in replacements for Conv2D and Dense; every prediction samples new weights.
  • Averaging repeated predictions improves accuracy, and their disagreement flags inputs the network does not know.
  • The cost is several forward passes per prediction. SNGP detects unfamiliar inputs in a single pass.

docs.title: Bayesian weather forecasting: what the model knows and what it doesn't
docs.text:
Backend: TensorFlow, JAX or PyTorch Dataset: Jena climate Techniques: Conv1DFlipout, DenseFlipout, GaussianHead

View in Colab GitHub source

Separate the noise in the weather from the model's own uncertainty, with Bayesian layers.

A forecast can be uncertain for two different reasons:

  • Aleatoric uncertainty: the weather is noisy. More data would not remove it.
  • Epistemic uncertainty: the model is unsure, e.g. because the input is unlike anything it was trained on. More data would reduce it.

A Bayesian layer learns a distribution over its weights instead of a single value. Every prediction samples new weights, so repeating a prediction gives slightly different forecasts: their spread is the epistemic uncertainty. Adding a GaussianHead on top also predicts the aleatoric part.

# Install keras-proba, then choose a backend: "jax", "tensorflow" or "torch".
!pip install -q keras-proba
import os

os.environ["KERAS_BACKEND"] = "jax"

docs.title: Load the data
docs.text:
As in the probabilistic forecasting example: predict the temperature 24 hours ahead from the last 48 hours of the Jena climate data, split in time. Here the inputs keep their time axis, (48 hours, 5 measurements), for a 1D convolution.

import glob

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

import keras
import keras_proba

keras.utils.set_random_seed(0)
LOOKBACK, HORIZON = 48, 24  # Hours.

path = keras.utils.get_file(
    origin="https://storage.googleapis.com/tensorflow/tf-keras-datasets/jena_climate_2009_2016.csv.zip",
    extract=True,
)
csv = glob.glob(os.path.join(path, "**", "*.csv"), recursive=True)[0]
data = np.genfromtxt(csv, delimiter=",", skip_header=1, usecols=(1, 2, 4, 5, 12), dtype="float32")[5::6]
data[:, 4] = np.maximum(data[:, 4], 0)  # -9999 marks missing wind measurements.
temperature = data[:, 1].copy()

train_end, val_end = int(0.7 * len(data)), int(0.85 * len(data))
features = (data - data[:train_end].mean(0)) / data[:train_end].std(0)


def windows(start, stop):
    """Inputs: the last 48 hours of features. Targets: the temperature 24 hours later."""
    ends = np.arange(max(start, LOOKBACK), stop - HORIZON + 1)
    x = np.stack([features[t - LOOKBACK : t] for t in ends])
    return x, temperature[ends + HORIZON - 1][:, None]


x_train, y_train = windows(0, train_end)
x_val, y_val = windows(train_end, val_end)
x_test, y_test = windows(val_end, len(data))

docs.title: A Bayesian model
docs.text:
Conv1DFlipout and DenseFlipout are the Bayesian versions of Conv1D and Dense. Training balances fitting the data against keeping the weight distributions close to a prior; kl_weight sets how much the prior counts, and 1 / number of training examples is the standard choice. Bayesian layers learn more slowly than standard ones, so we train for longer, with a higher learning rate.

kl_weight = 1.0 / len(x_train)
model = keras.Sequential(
    [
        keras.Input(x_train.shape[1:]),
        keras_proba.layers.Conv1DFlipout(32, 5, padding="same", activation="relu", kl_weight=kl_weight),
        keras_proba.layers.Conv1DFlipout(32, 5, strides=2, padding="same", activation="relu", kl_weight=kl_weight),
        keras.layers.Flatten(),
        keras_proba.layers.DenseFlipout(64, activation="relu", kl_weight=kl_weight),
        keras_proba.layers.GaussianHead(1),
    ]
)
model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(3e-3), loss=keras_proba.losses.GaussianNLL())
model.fit(
    x_train,
    y_train,
    validation_data=(x_val, y_val),
    epochs=40,
    batch_size=256,
    callbacks=[keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(patience=5, restore_best_weights=True)],
    verbose=0,
)

docs.title: Repeat the forecast to measure what the model doesn't know
docs.text:
Each predict call samples new weights. Over 30 calls:

  • the average of the predicted variances is the aleatoric uncertainty;
  • the variance of the predicted means is the epistemic uncertainty;

and their sum is the total predictive variance.

def forecast(x, num_samples=30):
    means, variances = [], []
    for _ in range(num_samples):
        mean, std = keras_proba.ops.split_gaussian_params(model.predict(x, batch_size=1024, verbose=0))
        means.append(keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(mean)[:, 0])
        variances.append(keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(std)[:, 0] ** 2)
    means, variances = np.array(means), np.array(variances)
    return means.mean(0), np.sqrt(variances.mean(0)), np.sqrt(means.var(0))


mean, aleatoric, epistemic = forecast(x_test)
total = np.sqrt(aleatoric**2 + epistemic**2)
print(f"Average uncertainty (°C): aleatoric {aleatoric.mean():.2f}, epistemic {epistemic.mean():.2f}")
print(f"90% intervals contain the actual temperature {np.mean(np.abs(y_test[:, 0] - mean) <= 1.645 * total):.1%} of the time")

hours = np.arange(24 * 10)
plt.figure(figsize=(9, 3))
plt.fill_between(hours, (mean - 1.645 * total)[hours], (mean + 1.645 * total)[hours], alpha=0.3, label="90% interval (total)")
plt.fill_between(hours, (mean - 1.645 * epistemic)[hours], (mean + 1.645 * epistemic)[hours], alpha=0.5, label="epistemic part")
plt.plot(hours, y_test[hours, 0], "k", lw=1, label="actual")
plt.xlabel("hour")
plt.ylabel("temperature (°C)")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

Average uncertainty (°C): aleatoric 3.04, epistemic 0.77
90% intervals contain the actual temperature 92.2% of the time

docs.text:
Epistemic uncertainty should grow when the inputs leave the range of the training data, e.g. after a sensor fault. We shift every measurement by 3 standard deviations: a standard network would forecast with unchanged confidence.

_, _, epistemic_shifted = forecast(x_test[:2000] + 3.0)
print(f"Epistemic uncertainty (°C): normal inputs {epistemic[:2000].mean():.2f}, shifted inputs {epistemic_shifted.mean():.2f}")

Epistemic uncertainty (°C): normal inputs 0.73, shifted inputs 2.86

  • Repeating predictions splits the uncertainty into noise in the data (aleatoric) and the model's own uncertainty (epistemic).
  • Epistemic uncertainty flags inputs unlike the training data, which a deterministic model, even with a GaussianHead, cannot do.

docs.title: Conformal prediction intervals for a weather forecaster
docs.text:
Backend: TensorFlow, JAX or PyTorch Dataset: Jena climate Techniques: SplitConformalRegressor

View in Colab GitHub source

Add intervals with a 90% coverage guarantee to any trained forecaster, after training.

Most forecasting models output a single number. Split conformal prediction adds an interval around it after training, with a simple recipe and a guarantee:

  1. Measure the forecast errors on data the model was not trained on (the calibration set).
  2. Find the error size that 90% of these errors stay below.
  3. Use it as the margin around every new forecast.

If future data behaves like the calibration data, the intervals contain the truth at least 90% of the time, whatever the model: no retraining, no assumption about the error distribution.

# Install keras-proba, then choose a backend: "jax", "tensorflow" or "torch".
!pip install -q keras-proba
import os

os.environ["KERAS_BACKEND"] = "jax"

docs.title: Load the data
docs.text:
Predict the temperature 24 hours ahead from the last 48 hours of the Jena climate data. We train on 2009-2014, calibrate on the following year, and test on the last year.

import glob

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

import keras
import keras_proba

keras.utils.set_random_seed(0)
LOOKBACK, HORIZON = 48, 24  # Hours.

path = keras.utils.get_file(
    origin="https://storage.googleapis.com/tensorflow/tf-keras-datasets/jena_climate_2009_2016.csv.zip",
    extract=True,
)
csv = glob.glob(os.path.join(path, "**", "*.csv"), recursive=True)[0]
data = np.genfromtxt(csv, delimiter=",", skip_header=1, usecols=(1, 2, 4, 5, 12), dtype="float32")[5::6]
data[:, 4] = np.maximum(data[:, 4], 0)  # -9999 marks missing wind measurements.
temperature = data[:, 1].copy()

train_end, cal_end = int(0.7 * len(data)), int(0.85 * len(data))
features = (data - data[:train_end].mean(0)) / data[:train_end].std(0)


def windows(start, stop):
    ends = np.arange(max(start, LOOKBACK), stop - HORIZON + 1)
    x = np.stack([features[t - LOOKBACK : t].reshape(-1) for t in ends])
    return x, temperature[ends + HORIZON - 1][:, None]


x_train, y_train = windows(0, train_end)
x_cal, y_cal = windows(train_end, cal_end)
x_test, y_test = windows(cal_end, len(data))

docs.title: A standard point forecaster
docs.text:
Any trained model works. This one is a plain regression network trained with the mean squared error: it forecasts a temperature, with no idea of how far off it might be.

model = keras.Sequential(
    [
        keras.Input((x_train.shape[1],)),
        keras.layers.Dense(128, activation="relu"),
        keras.layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"),
        keras.layers.Dense(1),
    ]
)
model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="mse")
model.fit(
    x_train,
    y_train,
    validation_split=0.2,
    epochs=15,
    batch_size=256,
    callbacks=[keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(patience=3, restore_best_weights=True)],
    verbose=0,
)
forecast_cal, forecast_test = model.predict(x_cal, verbose=0), model.predict(x_test, verbose=0)

docs.title: Calibrate the intervals
docs.text:
SplitConformalRegressor measures the absolute errors on the calibration year and keeps the threshold that 90% of them stay below. The histogram shows those errors and the threshold.

conformal = keras_proba.postprocessing.SplitConformalRegressor(alpha=0.1)  # alpha = 1 - 90%.
conformal.fit(y_cal, forecast_cal)
threshold = float(keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(conformal.quantile_)[0])

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 3))
plt.hist(np.abs(y_cal - forecast_cal)[:, 0], bins=80)
plt.axvline(threshold, color="r", label=f"threshold: 90% of errors are below {threshold:.1f} °C")
plt.xlabel("|forecast error| on the calibration year (°C)")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

docs.title: Forecast with intervals, and check them on the test year
docs.text:
Every forecast becomes forecast ± threshold. On the test year, unseen during training and calibration, the intervals should contain the actual temperature about 90% of the time.

lower, upper = conformal.predict_interval(forecast_test)
coverage = float(keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(keras_proba.postprocessing.interval_coverage(y_test, lower, upper))[0])
print(f"The 90% intervals contain the actual temperature {coverage:.1%} of the time on the test year")

lower, upper = keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(lower)[:, 0], keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(upper)[:, 0]
hours = np.arange(24 * 10)
plt.figure(figsize=(9, 3))
plt.fill_between(hours, lower[hours], upper[hours], alpha=0.3, label="90% conformal interval")
plt.plot(hours, forecast_test[hours, 0], label="forecast")
plt.plot(hours, y_test[hours, 0], "k", lw=1, label="actual")
plt.xlabel("hour")
plt.ylabel("temperature (°C)")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

The 90% intervals contain the actual temperature 91.1% of the time on the test year

docs.title: What we learned
docs.text:
• Conformal prediction turns a model's errors on held-out data into intervals with a coverage guarantee, after training and for any model.
  • The guarantee assumes the calibration data resembles future data. Weather changes from year to year, so calibrate on recent data and recalibrate regularly.
  • These intervals all have the same width. Passing a per-forecast uncertainty (scale=, e.g. from a GaussianHead) makes them adapt to each input: see conformal regression.

docs.title: Conformal prediction sets: "it's one of these"
docs.text:
Backend: TensorFlow, JAX or PyTorch Dataset: Fashion-MNIST, MNIST Techniques: SplitConformalClassifier

View in Colab GitHub source

Predict sets of classes that contain the true class 90% of the time, after training.

Instead of a single class, a prediction set lists every class the image could plausibly be, chosen so that the set contains the true class 90% of the time. Easy images get a single class; ambiguous ones (a shirt or a T-shirt?) get several. The size of the set is an honest, per-image measure of uncertainty.

Split conformal prediction builds these sets from any trained classifier, after training: calibrate a threshold on held-out images, then include every class that clears it.

# Install keras-proba, then choose a backend: "jax", "tensorflow" or "torch".
!pip install -q keras-proba
import os

os.environ["KERAS_BACKEND"] = "jax"

docs.title: Load the data
docs.text:
Fashion-MNIST: 10 classes of clothing. 10,000 training images are held out for calibration.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

import keras
import keras_proba

keras.utils.set_random_seed(0)
CLASSES = ["T-shirt", "trouser", "pullover", "dress", "coat", "sandal", "shirt", "sneaker", "bag", "boot"]
(x, y), (x_test, y_test) = keras.datasets.fashion_mnist.load_data()
x, x_test = x[..., None].astype("float32") / 255, x_test[..., None].astype("float32") / 255
x_cal, y_cal, x_train, y_train = x[:10_000], y[:10_000], x[10_000:], y[10_000:]

docs.title: Any trained classifier
docs.text:
A small CNN that outputs class probabilities.

model = keras.Sequential(
    [
        keras.Input((28, 28, 1)),
        keras.layers.Conv2D(32, 3, padding="same", activation="relu"),
        keras.layers.MaxPooling2D(),
        keras.layers.Conv2D(64, 3, padding="same", activation="relu"),
        keras.layers.MaxPooling2D(),
        keras.layers.Flatten(),
        keras.layers.Dropout(0.3),
        keras.layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax"),
    ]
)
model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy", metrics=["accuracy"])
model.fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=5, batch_size=128, verbose=0)
probs_cal, probs_test = model.predict(x_cal, verbose=0), model.predict(x_test, verbose=0)
print(f"Test accuracy of the most probable class: {(probs_test.argmax(-1) == y_test).mean():.1%}")

Test accuracy of the most probable class: 89.5%

docs.title: Calibrate and predict sets
docs.text:
SplitConformalClassifier with score="aps" adds classes from the most to the least probable until their total probability reaches a threshold calibrated on the held-out images. (score="lac" instead keeps every class above a fixed probability: smaller sets on average, but less adaptive.)

conformal = keras_proba.postprocessing.SplitConformalClassifier(alpha=0.1, score="aps", seed=0)
conformal.fit(y_cal, probs_cal)
sets = keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(conformal.predict_set(probs_test))  # (images, classes), True = in the set.

coverage = float(keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(keras_proba.postprocessing.set_coverage(y_test, sets)))
print(f"The sets contain the true class for {coverage:.1%} of the test images, with {sets.sum(-1).mean():.2f} classes on average")

The sets contain the true class for 89.9% of the test images, with 1.23 classes on average

docs.title: What the sets look like
docs.text:
Clear images get one class. Ambiguous images, often tops and shirts that look alike, get several: the set says exactly which classes the model cannot tell apart. (A few very confident images get an empty set: that is how the APS sets hit exactly 90% on average. Count an empty set as "probably the top class, but not guaranteed".)

size = sets.sum(-1)
examples = np.concatenate([np.flatnonzero(size == 1)[:4], np.argsort(size)[-4:]])  # Four single-class sets, four of the largest.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(11, 7))
for ax, i in zip(axes.flat, examples):
    ax.imshow(x_test[i, ..., 0], cmap="gray_r")
    members = [CLASSES[k] for k in np.flatnonzero(sets[i])]
    lines = [", ".join(members[j : j + 3]) for j in range(0, len(members), 3)]
    ax.set_title(f"true: {CLASSES[y_test[i]]}\nset: " + ",\n".join(lines), fontsize=9)
    ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

docs.title: Set size follows difficulty
docs.text:
Classes the model confuses get larger sets, and so do the images where its top prediction is wrong: exactly where a single answer would mislead.

correct = probs_test.argmax(-1) == y_test
size = sets.sum(-1)
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 3))
plt.bar(CLASSES, [size[y_test == k].mean() for k in range(10)])
plt.ylabel("mean set size")
plt.xticks(rotation=45)
plt.show()
print(f"Mean set size when the top prediction is right: {size[correct].mean():.2f}, when it is wrong: {size[~correct].mean():.2f}")


Mean set size when the top prediction is right: 1.14, when it is wrong: 2.02

docs.title: What we learned
docs.text:
• Conformal prediction turns any classifier's probabilities into sets that contain the true class 90% of the time, after training.
  • The set size is a per-image measure of uncertainty: one class for easy images, several for ambiguous ones.
  • The guarantee assumes the calibration images resemble the test images. Here they come from the training set, and the official test images are slightly harder, so the coverage can land a little below 90%.

docs.title: Adaptive conformal intervals for house prices
docs.text:
Backend: TensorFlow, JAX or PyTorch Dataset: California housing Techniques: GaussianHead, SplitConformalRegressor

View in Colab GitHub source

Make conformal intervals as wide as each prediction is uncertain, and keep their 90% guarantee.

Split conformal prediction gives intervals that contain the true value at least 90% of the time (see conformal forecast intervals for the recipe). Applied to a point prediction, every interval gets the same width. But some prices are much easier to predict than others: a fixed width is too wide for the easy ones and too narrow for the hard ones.

If the model also predicts its uncertainty, conformal prediction can measure the errors in units of that uncertainty. The intervals then stretch and shrink with each input, and keep their 90% guarantee.

# Install keras-proba, then choose a backend: "jax", "tensorflow" or "torch".
!pip install -q keras-proba
import os

os.environ["KERAS_BACKEND"] = "jax"

docs.title: Load the data
docs.text:
California housing: eight features per district and the median house value ($100,000 units). A quarter of the training data is held out for calibration.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

import keras
import keras_proba

keras.utils.set_random_seed(0)
(x, y), (x_test, y_test) = keras.datasets.california_housing.load_data(version="large")
y, y_test = (y / 1e5).astype("float32")[:, None], (y_test / 1e5).astype("float32")[:, None]
mean, std = x.mean(0), x.std(0)
x, x_test = (x - mean) / std, (x_test - mean) / std
x_cal, y_cal, x_train, y_train = x[: len(x) // 4], y[: len(x) // 4], x[len(x) // 4 :], y[len(x) // 4 :]

docs.title: A model that predicts its own uncertainty
docs.text:
A GaussianHead predicts a mean and a standard deviation for each district.

model = keras.Sequential(
    [
        keras.Input((8,)),
        keras.layers.Dense(128, activation="relu"),
        keras.layers.Dense(128, activation="relu"),
        keras_proba.layers.GaussianHead(1),
    ]
)
model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss=keras_proba.losses.GaussianNLL())
model.fit(
    x_train,
    y_train,
    validation_split=0.1,
    epochs=100,
    batch_size=128,
    callbacks=[keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(patience=10, restore_best_weights=True)],
    verbose=0,
)
mean_cal, std_cal = keras_proba.ops.split_gaussian_params(model.predict(x_cal, verbose=0))
mean_test, std_test = keras_proba.ops.split_gaussian_params(model.predict(x_test, verbose=0))

docs.title: Constant and adaptive conformal intervals
docs.text:
Both are calibrated on the same held-out districts. The only difference is scale=.

constant = keras_proba.postprocessing.SplitConformalRegressor(alpha=0.1).fit(y_cal, mean_cal)
adaptive = keras_proba.postprocessing.SplitConformalRegressor(alpha=0.1).fit(y_cal, mean_cal, scale=std_cal)
intervals = {
    "constant width": constant.predict_interval(mean_test),
    "adaptive width": adaptive.predict_interval(mean_test, scale=std_test),
}

for name, (lower, upper) in intervals.items():
    coverage = float(keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(keras_proba.postprocessing.interval_coverage(y_test, lower, upper))[0])
    width = float(keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(keras.ops.mean(upper - lower)))
    print(f"{name}: contains the actual value {coverage:.1%} of the time, mean width ${width * 100:.0f}k")

constant width: contains the actual value 91.0% of the time, mean width $166k
adaptive width: contains the actual value 90.0% of the time, mean width $147k

docs.title: Where do the intervals hold?
docs.text:
Both are valid on average, but prices are harder to predict in some groups of districts than in others. Split the districts by median income: the constant intervals cover some groups well above 90% and others below it. The adaptive intervals change their width from group to group, and keep every group close to 90%.

income = x_test[:, 0]
groups = np.digitize(income, np.quantile(income, [0.25, 0.5, 0.75]))
labels = ["lowest", "second", "third", "highest"]

fig, (ax_coverage, ax_width) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3))
for i, (name, (lower, upper)) in enumerate(intervals.items()):
    lower, upper = keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(lower)[:, 0], keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(upper)[:, 0]
    inside = (y_test[:, 0] >= lower) & (y_test[:, 0] <= upper)
    positions = np.arange(4) + 0.4 * i
    ax_coverage.bar(positions, [inside[groups == g].mean() for g in range(4)], width=0.4, label=name)
    ax_width.bar(positions, [100 * (upper - lower)[groups == g].mean() for g in range(4)], width=0.4, label=name)
ax_coverage.axhline(0.9, color="k", ls="--", lw=1)
ax_coverage.set(ylim=(0.75, 1.0), ylabel="coverage", xticks=np.arange(4) + 0.2, xticklabels=labels, xlabel="income quartile")
ax_width.set(ylabel="mean width ($k)", xticks=np.arange(4) + 0.2, xticklabels=labels, xlabel="income quartile")
ax_coverage.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

docs.title: What we learned
docs.text:
• Conformal intervals around a point prediction have a constant width, and are valid on average but uneven across inputs.
  • Giving SplitConformalRegressor the model's predicted standard deviation (scale=) keeps the 90% guarantee and makes the intervals adapt: narrower on average, and fairer across groups.
  • The scale can come from a GaussianHead, a MixtureGaussianHead (keras_proba.ops.mixture_mean_and_stddev) or the spread of a Bayesian model's predictions.

docs.title: House prices with a mixture density network
docs.text:
Backend: TensorFlow, JAX or PyTorch Dataset: California housing Techniques: GaussianHead, MixtureGaussianHead

View in Colab GitHub source

Predict the full distribution of house prices, including the spike at the census price cap.

Some targets do not follow a bell curve. In the California housing census, house values were capped at $500,001: about 5% of the districts sit exactly at the cap. A model predicting a single Gaussian has to smear its probability over that spike.

A mixture density network predicts a mixture of Gaussians for every input: several bumps, each with its own weight, center and width. It can put a narrow bump on the cap and a wide one elsewhere. In keras_proba it is the MixtureGaussianHead, trained with MixtureGaussianNLL.

# Install keras-proba, then choose a backend: "jax", "tensorflow" or "torch".
!pip install -q keras-proba
import os

os.environ["KERAS_BACKEND"] = "jax"

docs.title: Load the data
docs.text:
Eight features per district (median income, house age, rooms, location, ...) and the median house value, in units of $100,000.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

import keras
import keras_proba

keras.utils.set_random_seed(0)
CAP = 5.00001  # $500,001.

(x_train, y_train), (x_test, y_test) = keras.datasets.california_housing.load_data(version="large")
y_train, y_test = (y_train / 1e5).astype("float32")[:, None], (y_test / 1e5).astype("float32")[:, None]
mean, std = x_train.mean(0), x_train.std(0)
x_train, x_test = (x_train - mean) / std, (x_test - mean) / std

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 3))
plt.hist(y_train[:, 0], bins=100)
plt.xlabel("median house value ($100k)")
plt.title("The spike at the right is the $500k cap")
plt.show()

docs.title: Train a single Gaussian and a mixture
docs.text:
The same network, with two different output layers: GaussianHead predicts one Gaussian; MixtureGaussianHead(num_components=5) predicts a mixture of five.

def train(head, loss):
    model = keras.Sequential(
        [keras.Input((8,)), keras.layers.Dense(128, activation="relu"), keras.layers.Dense(128, activation="relu"), head]
    )
    model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss=loss)
    model.fit(
        x_train,
        y_train,
        validation_split=0.1,
        epochs=100,
        batch_size=128,
        callbacks=[keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(patience=10, restore_best_weights=True)],
        verbose=0,
    )
    return model


gaussian = train(keras_proba.layers.GaussianHead(1), keras_proba.losses.GaussianNLL())
mixture = train(keras_proba.layers.MixtureGaussianHead(num_components=5), keras_proba.losses.MixtureGaussianNLL())

docs.title: Which model explains the prices better?
docs.text:
The negative log-likelihood (NLL) measures how probable the true prices are under each predicted distribution: lower is better. The difference is largest for the districts at the cap.

gaussian_nll = keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(keras_proba.losses.gaussian_nll(y_test, gaussian.predict(x_test, verbose=0)))
mixture_nll = keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(keras_proba.losses.mixture_gaussian_nll(y_test, mixture.predict(x_test, verbose=0)))
capped = y_test[:, 0] >= CAP - 1e-3
print(f"Test NLL, all districts:     Gaussian {gaussian_nll.mean():.2f}, mixture {mixture_nll.mean():.2f}")
print(f"Test NLL, districts at cap:  Gaussian {gaussian_nll[capped].mean():.2f}, mixture {mixture_nll[capped].mean():.2f}")

Test NLL, all districts:     Gaussian 0.60, mixture 0.36
Test NLL, districts at cap:  Gaussian 1.91, mixture 0.28

docs.title: Look at one predicted distribution
docs.text:
For a district at the cap, the single Gaussian can only stretch its one bell curve, which puts probability on values above the cap that never occur. The mixture adds a separate bump at the cap itself.

def density(params, values, mixture_model):
    if mixture_model:
        logits, means, scales = (keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(t)[0] for t in keras_proba.ops.split_mixture_params(params))
        weights = np.exp(logits) / np.exp(logits).sum()
        means, scales = means[:, 0], scales[:, 0]
    else:
        mean, scale = (keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(t)[0] for t in keras_proba.ops.split_gaussian_params(params))
        weights, means, scales = np.ones(1), mean, scale
    gaussians = np.exp(-0.5 * ((values[:, None] - means) / scales) ** 2) / (scales * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi))
    return gaussians @ weights


# One of the districts at the cap where the mixture puts the most probability near the cap.
mixture_params = mixture.predict(x_test[capped], verbose=0)
near_cap = [density(mixture_params[i : i + 1], np.array([CAP]), True)[0] for i in range(len(mixture_params))]
district = np.flatnonzero(capped)[int(np.argmax(near_cap))]
values = np.linspace(0, 7, 500)
plt.figure(figsize=(7, 3))
plt.plot(values, density(gaussian.predict(x_test[district : district + 1], verbose=0), values, False), label="single Gaussian")
plt.plot(values, density(mixture.predict(x_test[district : district + 1], verbose=0), values, True), label="mixture of 5")
plt.axvline(y_test[district, 0], color="k", ls="--", label="actual value (the cap)")
plt.xlabel("median house value ($100k)")
plt.ylabel("predicted density")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

docs.title: What we learned
docs.text:
• A mixture density network predicts a full distribution, which can have several modes or spikes that a single Gaussian cannot represent.
  • MixtureGaussianHead and MixtureGaussianNLL are drop-in replacements for GaussianHead and GaussianNLL. keras_proba.ops.mixture_mean_and_stddev gives the predictive mean and spread.
  • Mixtures can get stuck covering only some of the modes: ReLU features and a modest learning rate train them reliably.

docs.title: Probabilistic weather forecasts from a pre-trained FourCastNet
docs.text:
Backend: TensorFlow, JAX or PyTorch Dataset: ERA5 (WeatherBench 2) Techniques: SplitConformalRegressor

View in Colab GitHub source

Turn a pre-trained global weather model into 90% forecast intervals at every point on Earth, without any training.

FourCastNet is a neural weather model from NVIDIA, trained on 40 years of ERA5 reanalysis data. From the state of the atmosphere now (20 variables on a 0.25° grid, about 1 million points), it predicts the state 6 hours later. keras-climate provides it as a Keras model with NVIDIA's original weights.

Like most weather models, it outputs a single forecast, with no indication of how far off it might be. Here we add that, with no training at all:

  1. Run the pre-trained model on past days, and compare its forecasts with what actually happened.
  2. At every grid point, find the error size that 90% of these errors stay below (split conformal prediction).
  3. Use it as the margin around every new forecast at that point.

Runtime: use a GPU (Runtime → Change runtime type → T4 GPU on Colab). The notebook downloads the model (0.9 GB) and 30 days of ERA5 data (about 3 GB), and runs the model 120 times.

# Install keras-proba and keras-climate, then choose a backend: "jax", "tensorflow" or "torch".
# PyTorch is also needed, to read NVIDIA's original checkpoint (it is preinstalled on Colab).
!pip install -q keras-proba "keras-climate>=0.1.1" ruamel.yaml xarray zarr gcsfs
import os

os.environ["KERAS_BACKEND"] = "jax"

docs.title: Load the pre-trained model
docs.text:
fourcastnet_backbone downloads NVIDIA's checkpoint and loads it into the Keras model. The model works on standardized variables, so we also download the mean and standard deviation of each variable that it was trained with.

import io
import urllib.request

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import xarray as xr

import keras
import keras_proba
from keras_climate.weights.pretrained import fourcastnet_backbone

model, _ = fourcastnet_backbone()

STATS_URL = "https://portal.nersc.gov/project/m4134/FCN_weights_v0/stats_v0/"
means = np.load(io.BytesIO(urllib.request.urlopen(STATS_URL + "global_means.npy").read()))[0, :20, 0, 0]
stds = np.load(io.BytesIO(urllib.request.urlopen(STATS_URL + "global_stds.npy").read()))[0, :20, 0, 0]

[keras_climate] converted 148/148 weights.

docs.title: Load the weather data
docs.text:
WeatherBench 2 hosts ERA5 on Google Cloud, readable without an account. load_state reads the 20 variables FourCastNet expects, in its order, on its 720 × 1440 grid (latitudes 90° to -89.75°).

ERA5 = "gs://weatherbench2/datasets/era5/1959-2023_01_10-wb13-6h-1440x721_with_derived_variables.zarr"
era5 = xr.open_zarr(ERA5, storage_options={"token": "anon"})

# FourCastNet's 20 input variables: (ERA5 name, pressure level in hPa, or None at the surface).
VARIABLES = [
    ("10m_u_component_of_wind", None), ("10m_v_component_of_wind", None), ("2m_temperature", None),
    ("surface_pressure", None), ("mean_sea_level_pressure", None), ("temperature", 850),
    ("u_component_of_wind", 1000), ("v_component_of_wind", 1000), ("geopotential", 1000),
    ("u_component_of_wind", 850), ("v_component_of_wind", 850), ("geopotential", 850),
    ("u_component_of_wind", 500), ("v_component_of_wind", 500), ("geopotential", 500),
    ("temperature", 500), ("geopotential", 50), ("relative_humidity", 500), ("relative_humidity", 850),
    ("total_column_water_vapour", None),
]
T2M = 2  # Index of the 2 m temperature, the variable we forecast with intervals.


def load_state(time):
    snapshot = era5.sel(time=time)
    loaded, state = {}, []
    for name, level in VARIABLES:
        if name not in loaded:
            loaded[name] = snapshot[name].load()  # All its pressure levels, in one request.
        field = loaded[name] if level is None else loaded[name].sel(level=level)
        state.append(field.values[:720])
    state = np.stack(state, axis=-1)
    state[..., 17:19] *= 100  # Relative humidity: a fraction in WeatherBench 2, a percentage for FourCastNet.
    return state.astype("float32")


def load_t2m(time):
    return era5["2m_temperature"].sel(time=time).values[:720].astype("float32")

docs.title: Forecast 24 hours ahead
docs.text:
Each model step advances the atmosphere by 6 hours, so 4 steps give a 24-hour forecast. We keep the 2 m temperature, in °C.

def forecast_t2m(state, steps=4):
    x = ((state - means) / stds)[None]
    for _ in range(steps):
        x = model.predict(x, verbose=0)
    return x[0, ..., T2M] * stds[T2M] + means[T2M] - 273.15


# Grid-cell areas shrink towards the poles: weight averages by cos(latitude).
latitudes = np.linspace(90, -89.75, 720)
area = np.cos(np.deg2rad(latitudes))[:, None] * np.ones((1, 1440))
area /= area.mean()

docs.title: Run the model on past days
docs.text:
We forecast every day of January 2020 at 00 UTC: the first 20 days to calibrate the intervals, the last 10 to test them. For each forecast we also load the temperature that was actually observed 24 hours later. This is the slow part of the notebook.

days = np.arange("2020-01-01T00", "2020-01-31T00", np.timedelta64(1, "D"), dtype="datetime64[h]")
forecasts, actual, persistence = [], [], []
for day in days:
    state = load_state(day)
    forecasts.append(forecast_t2m(state))
    actual.append(load_t2m(day + np.timedelta64(24, "h")) - 273.15)
    persistence.append(state[..., T2M] - 273.15)  # Baseline: "tomorrow will be like today".
forecasts, actual, persistence = np.stack(forecasts), np.stack(actual), np.stack(persistence)

rmse = lambda prediction: np.sqrt(np.mean(area * (prediction - actual) ** 2))
print(f"24-hour forecast error (RMSE): FourCastNet {rmse(forecasts):.2f} °C, 'same as today' {rmse(persistence):.2f} °C")

24-hour forecast error (RMSE): FourCastNet 1.02 °C, 'same as today' 2.19 °C

docs.title: Calibrate the intervals
docs.text:
SplitConformalRegressor treats each grid point as its own output: for each, it measures the absolute errors on the 20 calibration days and keeps a threshold that at least 90% of future errors should stay below. With 20 days, this is the second largest of the 20 errors (conformal prediction rounds up, so that the guarantee holds with few calibration examples).

CALIBRATION = 20
y_cal = actual[:CALIBRATION].reshape(CALIBRATION, -1)  # (days, grid points)
f_cal = forecasts[:CALIBRATION].reshape(CALIBRATION, -1)

conformal = keras_proba.postprocessing.SplitConformalRegressor(alpha=0.1)  # alpha = 1 - 90%.
conformal.fit(y_cal, f_cal)
half_width = keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(conformal.quantile_).reshape(720, 1440)

The map shows the margin around every forecast. It is small over the oceans, where the temperature changes slowly, and large over land: most of all over the northern continents in winter, where cold air masses come and go, and over the Antarctic ice sheet.

land = era5["land_sea_mask"].values[:720]
extent = [-180, 180, -89.75, 90]
centered = lambda field: np.roll(field, 720, axis=-1)  # Longitudes 0..360 -> -180..180.

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 4.5))
plt.imshow(centered(half_width), extent=extent, cmap="Blues", vmin=0, vmax=np.percentile(half_width, 99))
plt.colorbar(label="interval half-width (°C)", shrink=0.8)
plt.contour(np.linspace(-180, 180, 1440), latitudes, centered(land), levels=[0.5], colors="k", linewidths=0.4)
plt.title("90% interval: forecast ± this margin, for the 24-hour temperature forecast")
plt.xlabel("longitude")
plt.ylabel("latitude")
plt.show()

docs.title: Check the intervals on the test days
docs.text:
On the 10 test days, unseen during calibration, the intervals should contain the observed temperature about 90% of the time.

f_test = forecasts[CALIBRATION:].reshape(len(days) - CALIBRATION, -1)
y_test = actual[CALIBRATION:].reshape(len(days) - CALIBRATION, -1)
lower, upper = conformal.predict_interval(f_test)
covered = keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(keras_proba.postprocessing.interval_coverage(y_test, lower, upper))
covered = covered.reshape(720, 1440)  # Fraction of the test days covered, at each grid point.
print(f"The 90% intervals contain the observed temperature {np.mean(area * covered):.1%} of the time (area-weighted)")

The 90% intervals contain the observed temperature 90.2% of the time (area-weighted)

Finally, the forecasts and intervals at three cities, through the test days. The black dots are the temperatures that were actually observed.

cities = {"Moscow": (55.75, 37.6), "Chicago": (41.9, -87.6), "Singapore": (1.35, 103.8)}
lower = keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(lower).reshape(-1, 720, 1440)
upper = keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(upper).reshape(-1, 720, 1440)
test_days = days[CALIBRATION:] + np.timedelta64(24, "h")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.5))
for ax, (city, (lat, lon)) in zip(axes, cities.items()):
    i, j = int(round((90 - lat) * 4)), int(round((lon % 360) * 4))
    dates = test_days.astype("datetime64[D]")
    ax.fill_between(dates, lower[:, i, j], upper[:, i, j], alpha=0.3, label="90% interval")
    ax.plot(dates, forecasts[CALIBRATION:, i, j], label="forecast")
    ax.plot(dates, actual[CALIBRATION:, i, j], "ko", ms=4, label="observed")
    ax.set(title=city, ylabel="temperature (°C)")
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=45)
axes[0].legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

docs.title: What we learned
docs.text:
• A pre-trained model's single forecast becomes a forecast with an interval, with no training: only its errors on a few past days are needed.
  • Each grid point gets its own margin, so the intervals are wide where the weather is hard to predict and narrow where it is not.
  • The guarantee holds when the calibration days resemble the forecast days. Weather depends on the season, so calibrate on recent days, for the same time of day and forecast lead time, and recalibrate as the season changes.
  • The guarantee is for each grid point on average over days, not for the whole map at once: on any given day, some regions will fall outside their intervals.

docs.title: Probabilistic weather forecasting with a Gaussian head
docs.text:
Backend: TensorFlow, JAX or PyTorch Dataset: Jena climate Techniques: GaussianHead

View in Colab GitHub source

Forecast tomorrow's temperature together with how sure the forecast is. A standard regression network predicts a single number. Here the network predicts a mean and a standard deviation for every forecast, so it can say "12 °C ± 1" on a stable day and "12 °C ± 4" when the weather is changing.

The output layer is a GaussianHead, trained with the Gaussian negative log-likelihood (GaussianNLL): the loss rewards an accurate mean, and a standard deviation that matches the actual errors.

# Install keras-proba, then choose a backend: "jax", "tensorflow" or "torch".
!pip install -q keras-proba
import os

os.environ["KERAS_BACKEND"] = "jax"

docs.title: Load the data
docs.text:
The Jena climate dataset has weather measurements every 10 minutes from 2009 to 2016. We keep one sample per hour and predict the temperature 24 hours ahead from the last 48 hours of pressure, temperature, dew point, humidity and wind. The data is split in time: 2009-2014 for training, the next year for validation and the last year for testing.

import glob

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

import keras
import keras_proba

keras.utils.set_random_seed(0)
LOOKBACK, HORIZON = 48, 24  # Hours.

path = keras.utils.get_file(
    origin="https://storage.googleapis.com/tensorflow/tf-keras-datasets/jena_climate_2009_2016.csv.zip",
    extract=True,
)
csv = glob.glob(os.path.join(path, "**", "*.csv"), recursive=True)[0]
data = np.genfromtxt(csv, delimiter=",", skip_header=1, usecols=(1, 2, 4, 5, 12), dtype="float32")[5::6]
data[:, 4] = np.maximum(data[:, 4], 0)  # -9999 marks missing wind measurements.
temperature = data[:, 1].copy()

train_end, val_end = int(0.7 * len(data)), int(0.85 * len(data))
features = (data - data[:train_end].mean(0)) / data[:train_end].std(0)


def windows(start, stop):
    """Inputs: the last 48 hours of features, flattened. Targets: the temperature 24 hours later."""
    ends = np.arange(max(start, LOOKBACK), stop - HORIZON + 1)
    x = np.stack([features[t - LOOKBACK : t].reshape(-1) for t in ends])
    return x, temperature[ends + HORIZON - 1][:, None]


x_train, y_train = windows(0, train_end)
x_val, y_val = windows(train_end, val_end)
x_test, y_test = windows(val_end, len(data))
print(f"{len(x_train)} training, {len(x_val)} validation and {len(x_test)} test forecasts")

48992 training, 10491 validation and 10491 test forecasts

docs.title: Build and train the model
docs.text:
The only change from a standard regression network is the output layer: GaussianHead(1) outputs [mean, std] for one target, and GaussianNLL trains both.

model = keras.Sequential(
    [
        keras.Input((x_train.shape[1],)),
        keras.layers.Dense(128, activation="relu"),
        keras.layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"),
        keras_proba.layers.GaussianHead(1),
    ]
)
model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss=keras_proba.losses.GaussianNLL())
model.fit(
    x_train,
    y_train,
    validation_data=(x_val, y_val),
    epochs=15,
    batch_size=256,
    callbacks=[keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(patience=3, restore_best_weights=True)],
    verbose=0,
)

<keras.src.callbacks.history.History at 0x7410152e7770>

docs.title: Forecasts with uncertainty
docs.text:
split_gaussian_params splits the output into the mean and the standard deviation. A 90% interval is the mean ± 1.645 standard deviations. The band is narrow when the weather is predictable and widens when it is not.

mean, std = keras_proba.ops.split_gaussian_params(model.predict(x_test, verbose=0))
mean, std = keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(mean)[:, 0], keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(std)[:, 0]

hours = np.arange(24 * 10)  # The first 10 days of the test year.
plt.figure(figsize=(9, 3))
plt.fill_between(hours, (mean - 1.645 * std)[hours], (mean + 1.645 * std)[hours], alpha=0.3, label="90% interval")
plt.plot(hours, mean[hours], label="forecast")
plt.plot(hours, y_test[hours, 0], "k", lw=1, label="actual")
plt.xlabel("hour")
plt.ylabel("temperature (°C)")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

docs.title: Are the intervals trustworthy?
docs.text:
An X% interval should contain the true temperature X% of the time. We check this on the test year, which the model has never seen.

for level, z in [(0.5, 0.674), (0.8, 1.282), (0.95, 1.960)]:
    coverage = np.mean(np.abs(y_test[:, 0] - mean) <= z * std)
    print(f"{level:.0%} interval: contains the actual temperature {coverage:.1%} of the time")

50% interval: contains the actual temperature 50.3% of the time
80% interval: contains the actual temperature 80.6% of the time
95% interval: contains the actual temperature 94.8% of the time

docs.title: What we learned
docs.text:
• A GaussianHead turns a regression network into one that predicts its own uncertainty, at the cost of one extra output.
  • The predicted intervals contain the actual temperature close to as often as they claim, often slightly less: the test year differs a little from the training years.
  • The standard deviation only describes the noise seen during training (aleatoric uncertainty). It cannot tell when the model itself is out of its depth: see Bayesian forecasting for that, and conformal forecast intervals for intervals with a coverage guarantee.

docs.title: Detecting unfamiliar inputs with SNGP
docs.text:
Backend: TensorFlow, JAX or PyTorch Dataset: Fashion-MNIST, MNIST Techniques: SpectralNormalization, GaussianProcessClassificationHead, ResetCovarianceCallback

View in Colab GitHub source

Make a classifier's confidence drop on inputs unlike its training data, in a single forward pass.

Show a clothing classifier a handwritten digit and it will still answer, often with high confidence: a standard network has no notion of "I have never seen anything like this".

The Spectral-normalized Neural Gaussian Process (SNGP) makes a network distance aware with two changes:

  1. SpectralNormalization on the hidden layers, so that inputs far apart stay far apart in the hidden features;
  2. a Gaussian process output layer, whose confidence drops with the distance from the training data (GaussianProcessClassificationHead).

We train both networks on Fashion-MNIST, then show them MNIST digits they have never seen.

# Install keras-proba, then choose a backend: "jax", "tensorflow" or "torch".
!pip install -q keras-proba
import os

os.environ["KERAS_BACKEND"] = "jax"

docs.title: Load the data
docs.text:
Fashion-MNIST images of clothing (10 classes) for training and testing, and MNIST digits as unfamiliar inputs.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

import keras
import keras_proba

(x_train, y_train), (x_test, y_test) = keras.datasets.fashion_mnist.load_data()
(_, _), (x_digits, _) = keras.datasets.mnist.load_data()
x_train, x_test, x_digits = (images.reshape(len(images), -1).astype("float32") / 255 for images in (x_train, x_test, x_digits))

docs.title: Two networks with the same backbone
docs.text:
A residual multi-layer network. The SNGP version wraps each hidden layer in SpectralNormalization and replaces the output layer with the Gaussian process head.

def build(sngp):
    inputs = keras.Input((784,))
    hidden = keras.layers.Dense(256)(inputs)
    for _ in range(3):
        layer = keras.layers.Dense(256, activation="relu")
        if sngp:
            layer = keras_proba.layers.SpectralNormalization(layer, norm_multiplier=0.95, mode="reparameterization")
        hidden = hidden + keras.layers.Dropout(0.1)(layer(hidden))
    if sngp:
        logits = keras_proba.layers.GaussianProcessClassificationHead(
            inner_dim=0, num_classes=10, scale_random_features=True, temperature=np.pi / 8, gp_cov_momentum=-1
        )(hidden)
    else:
        logits = keras.layers.Dense(10)(hidden)
    model = keras.Model(inputs, logits)
    model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss=keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True), metrics=["accuracy"])
    return model


keras.utils.set_random_seed(0)
standard = build(sngp=False)
standard.fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=10, batch_size=128, verbose=0)

keras.utils.set_random_seed(0)
sngp = build(sngp=True)
# The Gaussian process estimates its uncertainty from the training features; reset it at every
# epoch so that it reflects the final features.
sngp.fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=10, batch_size=128, verbose=0, callbacks=[keras_proba.callbacks.ResetCovarianceCallback()])

<keras.src.callbacks.history.History at 0x787e05b96c10>

docs.title: Confidence on clothing and on digits
docs.text:
The confidence of a prediction is its highest class probability. Both networks are about equally accurate on clothing, and confident on it. On digits, the standard network is often still confident; SNGP's confidence drops, mostly below 0.5.

def confidence(model, x):
    return keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(keras.ops.max(keras.ops.softmax(model.predict(x, batch_size=512, verbose=0)), axis=-1))


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3), sharey=True)
for ax, (name, model) in zip(axes, [("standard network", standard), ("SNGP", sngp)]):
    accuracy = (model.predict(x_test, batch_size=512, verbose=0).argmax(-1) == y_test).mean()
    ax.hist(confidence(model, x_test), bins=30, range=(0, 1), alpha=0.6, density=True, label="clothing (seen)")
    ax.hist(confidence(model, x_digits), bins=30, range=(0, 1), alpha=0.6, density=True, label="digits (never seen)")
    ax.set(title=f"{name}: accuracy {accuracy:.1%}", xlabel="confidence")
axes[0].legend()
plt.show()

docs.title: How well does the confidence separate digits from clothing?
docs.text:
The AUROC is the probability that a random digit gets a lower confidence than a random clothing image: 0.5 is chance, 1.0 is perfect separation.

def auroc(familiar, unfamiliar):
    ranks = np.concatenate([familiar, unfamiliar]).argsort().argsort() + 1
    n, m = len(familiar), len(unfamiliar)
    return (ranks[:n].sum() - n * (n + 1) / 2) / (n * m)


for name, model in [("standard network", standard), ("SNGP", sngp)]:
    print(f"{name}: AUROC {auroc(confidence(model, x_test), confidence(model, x_digits)):.3f}")

standard network: AUROC 0.809

SNGP: AUROC 0.926

docs.title: What we learned
docs.text:
• A standard network is confident even on inputs unlike anything it was trained on.
  • SNGP keeps the accuracy and makes the confidence drop for unfamiliar inputs, in a single forward pass: no ensembles, no repeated sampling.
  • The recipe: SpectralNormalization on the hidden layers, a GaussianProcessClassificationHead as output, and the ResetCovarianceCallback during training. See the SNGP guide for the details.

docs.title: Fixing an overconfident classifier with temperature scaling
docs.text:
Backend: TensorFlow, JAX or PyTorch Dataset: Fashion-MNIST, MNIST Techniques: TemperatureScaling

View in Colab GitHub source

Fix an overconfident image classifier after training, with a single parameter.

When a well-calibrated classifier says "95% sure", it is right 95% of the time. Modern networks trained to convergence are often overconfident: they say 95% but are right less often.

Temperature scaling fixes this after training by dividing the network's logits (its outputs before the softmax) by a single number, the temperature T:

  • T > 1 softens the probabilities (less confident);
  • the predicted class never changes, only how confident the prediction is.

T is fitted on held-out data, with TemperatureScaling.

# Install keras-proba, then choose a backend: "jax", "tensorflow" or "torch".
!pip install -q keras-proba
import os

os.environ["KERAS_BACKEND"] = "jax"

docs.title: Load the data
docs.text:
Fashion-MNIST: 10 classes of clothing. 10,000 training images are held out to fit the temperature.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

import keras
import keras_proba

keras.utils.set_random_seed(0)
(x, y), (x_test, y_test) = keras.datasets.fashion_mnist.load_data()
x, x_test = x[..., None].astype("float32") / 255, x_test[..., None].astype("float32") / 255

docs.title: Train a classifier until it is overconfident
docs.text:
A small CNN, trained for long enough to become overconfident. It outputs logits.

model = keras.Sequential(
    [
        keras.Input((28, 28, 1)),
        keras.layers.Conv2D(32, 3, padding="same", activation="relu"),
        keras.layers.MaxPooling2D(),
        keras.layers.Conv2D(64, 3, padding="same", activation="relu"),
        keras.layers.MaxPooling2D(),

        keras.layers.Dense(10),
    ]
)
model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss=keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True), metrics=["accuracy"])
model.fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=15, batch_size=128, verbose=0)
