docs.title: Fit the temperature
docs.text:
fit finds the temperature that makes the held-out predictions most probable. Appending the layer to the network gives the calibrated model.

scaling = keras_proba.postprocessing.TemperatureScaling()
temperature = scaling.fit(model.predict(x_val, verbose=0), y_val)
calibrated = keras.Sequential([model, scaling])
print(f"Fitted temperature: {temperature:.2f}")

Fitted temperature: 1.63

docs.title: Before and after: the reliability diagram
docs.text:
Group the test predictions by confidence, and compare each group's average confidence with how often it is right. A calibrated model lies on the diagonal. The expected calibration error (ECE) is the average gap, weighted by the number of predictions in each group.

def reliability(network, ax, title):
    logits = network.predict(x_test, batch_size=1024, verbose=0)
    probs = keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(keras.ops.softmax(logits))
    confidence, correct = probs.max(-1), probs.argmax(-1) == y_test
    ece = keras_proba.metrics.ExpectedCalibrationError(num_bins=10, from_logits=True)
    ece.update_state(y_test, logits)
    bins = np.minimum((confidence * 10).astype(int), 9)
    accuracy = [correct[bins == b].mean() if np.any(bins == b) else 0 for b in range(10)]
    ax.bar((np.arange(10) + 0.5) / 10, accuracy, width=0.1, edgecolor="k", label="accuracy")
    ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k--", label="perfect calibration")
    ax.set(title=f"{title}: ECE {float(keras.ops.convert_to_numpy(ece.result())):.3f}, accuracy {correct.mean():.1%}",
           xlabel="confidence", ylabel="accuracy")
    ax.legend()


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4), sharey=True)
reliability(model, axes[0], "before")
reliability(calibrated, axes[1], f"after (T = {temperature:.2f})")
plt.show()

docs.title: What we learned
docs.text:
• A network can be accurate and still overconfident: its confidence overstates how often it is right.
  • Temperature scaling fixes this with one parameter, fitted on held-out data in a fraction of a second, without changing any prediction.
  • ExpectedCalibrationError and BrierScore measure calibration, also during training with model.compile(metrics=...).

docs.title: Bayesian layers
docs.text:
Bayesian layers learn a distribution over their weights instead of a point estimate, with variational inference 1. Their predictions are stochastic: averaging several of them gives the predictive mean, and their spread is the model's (epistemic) uncertainty.

The layers are ports of TensorFlow Probability's tfp.layers, with its default distributions:

  • Posterior: a mean-field Normal \(q(W) = \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma = \epsilon + \mathrm{softplus}(\rho)\), initialized close to a point mass.
  • Prior: \(p(W) = \mathcal{N}(0, s^2)\) with kernel_prior_scale \(= s\) (default 1).
  • Bias: a point estimate.

Each call samples a kernel and adds kl_weight * KL(q(W) || p(W)) to the layer's losses, which model.fit adds to the training loss.

docs.title: Estimators
docs.text: Layers Estimator Notes DenseReparameterization, Conv{1,2,3}DReparameterization Reparameterization 2 One kernel sample per call, shared by the batch. DenseLocalReparameterization Local reparameterization 3 Samples the pre-activations directly, independently per example. DenseFlipout, Conv{1,2,3}DFlipout Flipout 4 Pseudo-independent perturbations per example with random signs: lower gradient variance, about twice the compute.

docs.title: Setting kl_weight
docs.text:
With the default mean loss over examples, the KL term must be counted once per epoch: set kl_weight = 1 / num_train_examples. With kl_weight=1 (the TFP default), the prior dominates and the posterior stays close to it.

import numpy as np
import keras
from keras_proba import layers

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.uniform(-2, 2, size=(512, 1)).astype("float32")
y = (np.sin(2 * x) + rng.normal(size=(512, 1)) * 0.1).astype("float32")

kl_weight = 1.0 / len(x)
model = keras.Sequential([
    keras.Input((1,)),
    layers.DenseFlipout(64, activation="relu", kl_weight=kl_weight),
    layers.DenseFlipout(64, activation="relu", kl_weight=kl_weight),
    layers.DenseFlipout(1, kl_weight=kl_weight),
])
model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(0.01), loss="mse")
model.fit(x, y, epochs=20, batch_size=64, verbose=0)

docs.title: Monte Carlo prediction
docs.text:
Every predict call draws fresh weights, on every backend, so the predictive distribution is a loop away:

x_test = np.linspace(-4, 4, 50, dtype="float32")[:, None]
samples = np.stack([model.predict(x_test, verbose=0) for _ in range(30)])
mean, epistemic_std = samples.mean(0), samples.std(0)  # The spread grows outside [-2, 2].

Pass seed= to a layer for reproducible samples.

docs.title: Convolutions
docs.text:
Conv1D, Conv2D and Conv3D variants take the usual filters, kernel_size, strides, padding ("valid" or "same"), data_format and dilation_rate:

model = keras.Sequential([
    keras.Input((28, 28, 1)),
    layers.Conv2DFlipout(16, 3, padding="same", activation="relu", kl_weight=1e-4),
    keras.layers.MaxPooling2D(),
    keras.layers.Flatten(),
    layers.DenseFlipout(10, kl_weight=1e-4),
])

Differences from TFP

  • The posterior and prior are fixed to TFP's defaults and configured with plain arguments, instead of arbitrary tfd distribution functions.
  • kl_weight replaces passing a custom divergence function to scale the KL term.
  • DenseLocalReparameterization adds the smallest positive float under its square root: in TFP, an all-zero input (e.g. after a ReLU) makes the scale gradient NaN.

  1. Charles Blundell et al. Weight Uncertainty in Neural Networks. ICML 2015. ↩

  2. Diederik Kingma, Max Welling. Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes. ICLR 2014. ↩

  3. Diederik Kingma, Tim Salimans, Max Welling. Variational Dropout and the Local Reparameterization Trick. NeurIPS 2015. ↩

  4. Yeming Wen et al. Flipout: Efficient Pseudo-Independent Weight Perturbations on Mini-Batches. ICLR 2018. ↩

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text: A classifier is calibrated when its confidence matches its accuracy: among predictions made with 80% confidence, 80% are correct. Modern networks are often overconfident 1.

docs.title: Measuring calibration
docs.text:
ExpectedCalibrationError bins predictions by confidence and averages the gap between confidence and accuracy per bin; BrierScore is a proper scoring rule for the whole predicted distribution. Both accumulate over batches, so evaluate gives the value on the whole dataset:

import numpy as np
import keras
from keras_proba import metrics, postprocessing

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.normal(size=(2300, 10)).astype("float32")
y = (1.5 * x[:, :3] + rng.gumbel(size=(2300, 3))).argmax(-1)
(x_train, y_train), (x_val, y_val), (x_test, y_test) = (x[:300], y[:300]), (x[300:1300], y[300:1300]), (x[1300:], y[1300:])

model = keras.Sequential([keras.Input((10,)), keras.layers.Dense(128, activation="relu"), keras.layers.Dense(3)])
model.compile(
    optimizer="adam",
    loss=keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True),
    metrics=[metrics.ExpectedCalibrationError(num_bins=15, from_logits=True), metrics.BrierScore(from_logits=True)],
)
model.fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=100, verbose=0)  # Overfits, so becomes overconfident.
print(model.evaluate(x_test, y_test, verbose=0, return_dict=True))

The metrics take probabilities or logits (from_logits), sparse or one-hot labels, and a single sigmoid output for binary classification. The functions expected_calibration_error, expected_calibration_error_quantiles (equal-count bins) and brier_decomposition (uncertainty, resolution and reliability) evaluate a full set of predictions at once.

docs.title: Temperature scaling
docs.text:
TemperatureScaling divides the logits of a trained model by a single temperature \(T\), fitted to minimize the negative log-likelihood on held-out data. It changes the confidence, never the predicted class:

scaling = postprocessing.TemperatureScaling()
temperature = scaling.fit(model.predict(x_val, verbose=0), y_val)  # > 1 for an overconfident model.
calibrated = keras.Sequential([model, scaling])
calibrated.compile(
    loss=keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True),
    metrics=[metrics.ExpectedCalibrationError(num_bins=15, from_logits=True)],
)
print(temperature, calibrated.evaluate(x_test, y_test, verbose=0, return_dict=True))

fit finds the exact optimum: the NLL is convex in \(1 / T\), so it is minimized by bisection in float64, with the same result on every backend and no learning rate to tune. The layer can also be trained with model.fit on a model whose other layers are frozen.

  1. Chuan Guo, Geoff Pleiss, Yu Sun, Kilian Q. Weinberger. On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks. ICML 2017. arXiv:1706.04599 ↩

docs.title: Conformal prediction
docs.text:
Split conformal prediction 1 2 turns any trained model into one with prediction intervals (regression) or prediction sets (classification) that contain the true label with probability at least \(1 - \alpha\). The only assumption is that calibration and test examples are exchangeable, e.g. drawn from the same distribution.

  1. Compute a nonconformity score \(s_i\) for each of \(n\) held-out calibration examples.
  2. Take \(\hat{q}\), the \(k\)-th smallest score, with \(k = \lceil (n + 1)(1 - \alpha) \rceil\).
  3. For a test input, return every label whose score is at most \(\hat{q}\).

The expected coverage is then exactly \(k / (n + 1)\) for continuous scores, between \(1 - \alpha\) and \(1 - \alpha + 1 / (n + 1)\).

The exact order statistic

keras_proba uses the \(k\)-th smallest score. The widely used numpy.quantile(scores, k / n, method="higher") selects the next larger one, which over-covers.

docs.title: Regression
docs.text:
SplitConformalRegressor uses absolute residuals \(|y - \hat{y}|\), giving intervals of constant width:

import numpy as np
import keras
from keras_proba import layers, losses, ops, postprocessing

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.uniform(-3, 3, size=(4000, 1)).astype("float32")
y = (np.sin(x) + rng.normal(size=x.shape) * (0.1 + 0.4 * np.abs(x))).astype("float32")
(x_train, y_train), (x_cal, y_cal), (x_test, y_test) = [(x[s], y[s]) for s in (slice(0, 2000), slice(2000, 3000), slice(3000, None))]

model = keras.Sequential([keras.Input((1,)), keras.layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"), layers.GaussianHead(1)])
model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(0.005), loss=losses.GaussianNLL())
model.fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=20, batch_size=128, verbose=0)
mean_cal, scale_cal = ops.split_gaussian_params(model.predict(x_cal, verbose=0))
mean_test, scale_test = ops.split_gaussian_params(model.predict(x_test, verbose=0))

conformal = postprocessing.SplitConformalRegressor(alpha=0.1).fit(y_cal, mean_cal)
lower, upper = conformal.predict_interval(mean_test)
print(float(postprocessing.interval_coverage(y_test, lower, upper)[0]))  # ~0.9

With a per-example scale, the score is the normalized residual \(|y - \hat{y}| / \sigma\), and the intervals \(\hat{y} \pm \hat{q} \sigma\) adapt to each input: narrow where the noise is low, wide where it is high. The scale can come from a GaussianHead, a MixtureGaussianHead (ops.mixture_mean_and_stddev) or the spread of Monte Carlo samples of a Bayesian model:

conformal = postprocessing.SplitConformalRegressor(alpha=0.1).fit(y_cal, mean_cal, scale=scale_cal)
lower, upper = conformal.predict_interval(mean_test, scale=scale_test)

Each output dimension gets its own threshold, so coverage holds for each dimension.

docs.title: Classification
docs.text:
SplitConformalClassifier returns boolean prediction sets of shape (n, num_classes), with two scores:

score Sets Properties "lac" Classes with probability at least \(1 - \hat{q}\) Exact coverage and the smallest sets on average; can be empty for ambiguous inputs. "aps" 3 The most probable classes until their mass reaches \(\hat{q}\) Set size adapts to each input's difficulty. Randomized by default for exact coverage (set seed= for reproducibility). 
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
x = rng.normal(size=(3000, 2)).astype("float32")
y = (x @ rng.normal(size=(2, 5)) + rng.gumbel(size=(3000, 5))).argmax(-1)
classifier = keras.Sequential([keras.Input((2,)), keras.layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"), keras.layers.Dense(5, activation="softmax")])
classifier.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy")
classifier.fit(x[:2000], y[:2000], epochs=10, verbose=0)
probs_cal, probs_test = classifier.predict(x[2000:2500], verbose=0), classifier.predict(x[2500:], verbose=0)

conformal = postprocessing.SplitConformalClassifier(alpha=0.1, score="aps", seed=0).fit(y[2000:2500], probs_cal)
sets = conformal.predict_set(probs_test)
print(float(postprocessing.set_coverage(y[2500:], sets)), float(postprocessing.average_set_size(sets)))

Non-randomized APS

randomized=False gives the classic non-randomized APS sets, which are never empty but conservative. On a hard 5-class task (63% accuracy) with a 90% target, they covered 99.6% of labels with 3.7 classes per set, against 90.0% and 2.2 classes for randomized APS.

docs.text:
config = conformal.get_config()  # JSON-compatible, including the fitted threshold.
restored = postprocessing.SplitConformalClassifier.from_config(config)

  2. Anastasios N. Angelopoulos, Stephen Bates. A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction and Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification. arXiv:2107.07511 ↩

  3. Yaniv Romano, Matteo Sesia, Emmanuel J. Candès. Classification with Valid and Adaptive Coverage. NeurIPS 2020. arXiv:2006.02544 ↩

docs.title: Probabilistic regression
docs.text: A regression model trained with mean squared error predicts a single value. A probabilistic regression head predicts a distribution per input, so the model also learns how noisy each target is (aleatoric uncertainty), and it is trained by maximum likelihood.

docs.title: Gaussian head
docs.text:
GaussianHead predicts a mean and a standard deviation per output 1 2: \(y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu(x), \sigma(x)^2)\) with $\sigma = \mathrm{softplus}(\cdot) + $ min_scale. Its output is [mean, scale] concatenated on the last axis, so it trains with plain targets and GaussianNLL:

import numpy as np
import keras
from keras_proba import layers, losses, ops

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.uniform(-3, 3, size=(2048, 1)).astype("float32")
noise_std = 0.05 + 0.3 * np.abs(x)  # The noise grows with |x|.
y = (np.sin(x) + rng.normal(size=x.shape) * noise_std).astype("float32")

model = keras.Sequential([
    keras.Input((1,)),
    keras.layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"),
    keras.layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"),
    layers.GaussianHead(1),
])
model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(0.005), loss=losses.GaussianNLL())
model.fit(x, y, epochs=20, batch_size=128, verbose=0)

mean, scale = ops.split_gaussian_params(model.predict(x[:5], verbose=0))

The predicted scale tracks the true noise level, and mean ± 1.96 * scale is a 95% interval. For intervals with a guaranteed coverage, pass mean and scale to a conformal regressor.

docs.title: Mixture density network
docs.text:
A single Gaussian cannot represent targets with several modes, e.g. \(y = \pm x^2\). MixtureGaussianHead predicts a mixture of num_components Gaussians 3:

\[p(y \mid x) = \sum_k \pi_k(x) \prod_d \mathcal{N}(y_d; \mu_{kd}(x), \sigma_{kd}(x)^2)\] 
sign = np.where(rng.uniform(size=x.shape) < 0.5, -1.0, 1.0)
y_bimodal = (sign * x**2 + rng.normal(size=x.shape) * 0.1).astype("float32")

model = keras.Sequential([
    keras.Input((1,)),
    keras.layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"),
    keras.layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"),
    layers.MixtureGaussianHead(num_components=3),
])
model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(0.005), loss=losses.MixtureGaussianNLL())
model.fit(x, y_bimodal, epochs=20, batch_size=128, verbose=0)

params = model.predict(x[:5], verbose=0)
logits, means, scales = ops.split_mixture_params(params)  # (5, 3), (5, 3, 1), (5, 3, 1).
mean, stddev = ops.mixture_mean_and_stddev(params)  # Including the spread between components.

Training mixtures

Mixtures can get stuck covering only some of the modes. In our tests, tanh hidden layers at a learning rate of 0.005 saturated and missed a mode in about half the runs, while ReLU features recovered both modes in every run. Prefer ReLU-like features or a small learning rate.

The mixture NLL sums the log-densities of a multi-output target (its joint likelihood), while GaussianNLL averages them over outputs; they agree for one output and one component.

  1. David A. Nix, Andreas S. Weigend. Estimating the mean and variance of the target probability distribution. ICNN 1994. ↩

  2. Balaji Lakshminarayanan, Alexander Pritzel, Charles Blundell. Simple and Scalable Predictive Uncertainty Estimation using Deep Ensembles. NeurIPS 2017. ↩

  3. Christopher M. Bishop. Mixture Density Networks. Technical report, Aston University, 1994. ↩

docs.title: Distance-aware models (SNGP)
docs.text:
The Spectral-normalized Neural Gaussian Process (SNGP) 1 makes a deterministic network aware of the distance between a test input and its training data, so its predictions become uncertain away from the data. It needs two changes to a standard network:

  1. Spectral normalization of the hidden layers, so that distances in input space are preserved in feature space (the network is bi-Lipschitz).
  2. A Gaussian process output layer instead of a dense layer, whose predictive variance grows with the distance from the training features.

The layers are ports of TensorFlow Model Garden's official/nlp/modeling/layers.

docs.title: The Gaussian process output layer
docs.text:
RandomFeatureGaussianProcess approximates a GP with random Fourier features 2, \(\phi(x) = \sqrt{2 / D} \cos(x W + b)\), followed by a linear layer. During training it accumulates the posterior precision matrix of the output weights over minibatches (the Laplace approximation); at inference it also returns the predictive covariance:

import numpy as np
import keras
from keras_proba import callbacks, layers, ops

inputs = keras.Input((16,))
logits, covmat = layers.RandomFeatureGaussianProcess(units=3, num_inducing=256)(inputs)
model = keras.Model(inputs, [logits, covmat])

x = np.random.normal(size=(8, 16)).astype("float32")
logits, covmat = model.predict(x, verbose=0)  # (8, 3) and (8, 8).

# Uncertainty-adjusted logits: the mean-field approximation of the posterior predictive.
adjusted = ops.mean_field_logits(logits, covmat, mean_field_factor=np.pi / 8)

The covariance is an estimate over the features seen during training. Because the features change while the network trains, reset it at the start of every epoch, so that the final estimate only reflects the last epoch:

train_model = keras.Model(inputs, model.outputs[0])
train_model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss=keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True))
train_model.fit(x, np.zeros(8), epochs=2, verbose=0, callbacks=[callbacks.ResetCovarianceCallback()])

ResetCovarianceCallback finds every covariance layer in the model, including those nested in other layers. With gp_cov_momentum=-1, the precision matrix is the exact sum over one epoch instead of a moving average.

docs.title: Spectral normalization
docs.text:
SpectralNormalization wraps a Dense layer (and SpectralNormalizationConv2D a Conv2D) and bounds the spectral norm of its kernel by norm_multiplier, estimated with power iteration. It has two modes:

mode Training rule Backends "projection" (default) The kernel is projected to the norm bound before each step, as in the reference. Identical to the reference on TensorFlow and PyTorch. On JAX, assignments to trainable variables inside fit are discarded, so the projected kernel is not persisted between steps; a warning is shown. "reparameterization" The layer is called with \(W \cdot c / \sigma(W)\) and the gradient flows through \(\sigma\), as in PyTorch's spectral_norm. The kernel variable is never modified. Identical on every backend.

In both modes, inference uses a normalized kernel on every backend.

docs.title: The SNGP classification head
docs.text:
GaussianProcessClassificationHead combines both: a spectral-normalized pooling layer and a GP output layer. It returns raw logits during training (compatible with model.fit) and mean-field adjusted logits at inference (temperature is the mean-field factor). Pass return_covmat=True to also get the covariance.

The defaults are tuned for BERT features

The head's defaults follow the reference, which was designed for BERT encoders: a tanh pooler, layer normalization of the GP input and random features with a standard deviation of 0.05. On small dense inputs, these hide the distance from the data: in our tests, out-of-distribution confidence stayed at 0.77 to 0.98. For such inputs, use the setup of the SNGP paper: a distance-preserving backbone and

head = layers.GaussianProcessClassificationHead(
    inner_dim=0,                  # No tanh pooler.
    num_classes=2,
    normalize_input=False,        # Keep the input magnitude.
    scale_random_features=True,
    custom_random_features_initializer=keras.initializers.RandomNormal(stddev=1.0),
    temperature=np.pi / 8,
    mode="reparameterization",
)

docs.title: A complete recipe
docs.text:
A distance-preserving backbone (a frozen random projection and residual spectral-normalized blocks) with the head:

from keras_proba import layers

def build_sngp(num_classes, hidden=64, blocks=2):
    inputs = keras.Input((2,))
    h = keras.layers.Dense(hidden, trainable=False)(inputs)
    for _ in range(blocks):
        block = layers.SpectralNormalization(
            keras.layers.Dense(hidden, activation="relu"), norm_multiplier=0.9, mode="reparameterization"
        )
        h = h + block(h)
    logits = layers.GaussianProcessClassificationHead(
        inner_dim=0,
        num_classes=num_classes,
        num_inducing=1024,
        normalize_input=False,
        scale_random_features=True,
        custom_random_features_initializer=keras.initializers.RandomNormal(stddev=1.0),
        temperature=np.pi / 8,
        gp_cov_momentum=-1,
    )(h)
    return keras.Model(inputs, logits)

model = build_sngp(num_classes=2)
model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(0.01), loss=keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True))

On a two-moons dataset this reaches about 99% confidence in distribution, and 0.55 to 0.73 far from the data (0.5 is uniform), on every backend.

  1. Jeremiah Liu et al. Simple and Principled Uncertainty Estimation with Deterministic Deep Learning via Distance Awareness. NeurIPS 2020. arXiv:2006.10108 ↩

  2. Ali Rahimi, Benjamin Recht. Random Features for Large-Scale Kernel Machines. NeurIPS 2007. ↩
